title: Book one: debts
hookLine: Marcus lists what he learned from each person, his grandfather's gentleness, his mother's simple living (Meditations 1.1–3)

cards: The acknowledgments page usually sits at the back of a book. Thanks to my editor, my agent, my partner for putting up with me. It's easy to skip.
Marcus Aurelius's notebook opens with its acknowledgments, and they fill a whole chapter. They aren't thanks for help with the book. They're thanks for help with becoming a person.
Before a single piece of advice, he lists the people who shaped him, and exactly what each one gave. Today, book one: debts.

teach.b: Book one of the Meditations is seventeen short sections, and nearly every one starts the same way: from so-and-so, I learned this. It opens with his grandfather.

In George Long's 1862 translation: "From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and the government of my temper." Then his father, who died when Marcus was small, remembered for modesty and a manly character.
Then his mother, and this one is lovely.

From her he learned piety and generosity, to hold back not only from doing wrong but even from thinking it, and, in Long's words, "simplicity in my way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich."
An emperor, thanking his mother for teaching him to live simply. The list keeps going. A tutor who taught him to put up with work and want little.

A teacher named Rusticus who taught him to read carefully, not to settle for skimming, and who lent him the writings of Epictetus. Friends, philosophers, his adoptive father, the gods. Notice the order.
Marcus doesn't start with who he is. He starts with who he owes.
Every good habit traces back to a face: the opposite of the self-made man. And notice how specific he is. Not thanks, Mom.
Thanks for this exact thing. Gratitude gets real when it gets specific.
Your line is the question the whole book asks: from whom I learned.

how: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius, including people in modern Stoic practice, imitate book one by writing their own list of the people who formed them and the specific thing each one taught.

games.q: you're the emperor of Rome, starting a private notebook. what goes on the first page?
o: the people who shaped you, and what each gave.
games.why: Marcus begins with debts: grandfather, father, mother, tutors, friends, the gods. before anything he says about himself, he names who he owes.

practice: Let three people come, one at a time: a parent, a grandparent, a coach, a boss, a friend.

For each, be as exact as Marcus, not they were great but what, exactly, they gave you, like a way of laughing at trouble, showing up early, how to make soup. Say each one inside: from them, I learned this.
